questions.question: Describe how a star like the Sun changes after the hydrogen in its core runs out, up to the formation of a white dwarf.
questions.expected_answer: Fusion in the core stops, gravity makes the helium core contract and heat up, and hydrogen fuses in a shell around it. The extra energy makes the outer layers expand enormously and cool, so the star becomes a red giant. The core reaches about 100 million °C and helium fuses into carbon and oxygen. Eventually the outer layers are pushed off into space as a glowing shell called a planetary nebula. The exposed core becomes a white dwarf: Earth-sized, very dense, very hot at first, with no fusion, slowly cooling over billions of years.

questions.question: Explain why a red giant is brighter than the star was on the main sequence, even though its surface is cooler.
questions.expected_answer: Brightness depends on both surface temperature and surface area. Each square metre of the cooler red surface gives off less light, but the star has swollen to many times its original diameter, so its surface area is enormously larger; the total light given off is therefore much greater.

questions.question: Compare the death of the Sun with the death of a star 20 times the mass of the Sun.
questions.expected_answer: The Sun will become a red giant, gently shed its outer layers as a planetary nebula and leave a white dwarf that slowly cools. A star of 20 solar masses becomes a red supergiant, fuses elements up to iron in its core, then its core collapses and it explodes as a supernova, leaving a neutron star or a black hole and scattering heavy elements into space.
